title: Where Nothing Falls
blurb: Dagny finds a way to make a whole shaft hold still, but the cost of keeping a friend's secret is climbing faster than her weight.

blocks.text: The Weighman wrote my number in the league book and didn't close it. He turned back a page to last Monday, to where he'd told me the Settle was free, and read down my column again with the lamp tipped over it.
"Five Mondays, Miss Quillon," he said. "Heavier every one. I told you last week."
"You did."
"Did you go?"
"No."
He looked up then. He is a broad, careful man with a pencil behind his ear, and in five weeks I had never once seen him look at an Anchor's face. He looks at the scale and he looks at the book.
"Two stone two over your base," he said, "and not a Pin touched today. What are you doing at night?"
"Lying flat. On the boards at home. Every night."

That was true, and it was no use, and I knew exactly why. Flat boards drain match carry at half the rate they should, because of what I am, and they drain none of the rest. The rest was four stone now, a stone a week since the Coopers. It sat in my ankles on the scale plate, in my knees and in the small of my back, and the book could see two of it.
"Then you're not lying long enough," he said. "I've seen girls your size crack a foot by midsummer. The Settle would have that off you in an afternoon."

It would. That was what frightened me. A Settle bed would take the four stone out of me in four hours, and I would get up lighter than I had been since the Coopers. And somewhere in the first hour the grit on the ward floor would start across the boards toward my bed legs, and a nurse would see it, and they would keep me. Osk had never seen one come back.
"I'm counted," I said.

He held my eyes a moment longer. Then he made a small pencil mark in the margin beside my name, not a number, and closed the book. I didn't know what the mark meant. The cold came into the lining of the coat under my arms and stayed there the whole match.

Hal was on his crate by the Lip rail again, ribs strapped under his shirt, stood down for another week at least. Rafe sat beside him. The debt was ninety-six this morning. He'd told me at breakfast, very quietly, and then made a joke about the porridge, and I had let him.

At Tuesday's talk Dunnet had said all of it again, standing up, to every one of us by our full names. Lisbet had said, "Right. Move on." Hal had said, "Aye." Teague had sent nothing since. Dunnet said that was worse, and nobody argued.
Osk's chair stood back from the rail, where the winch had set it down. Grit had crept in and ringed its legs again. I saw it and didn't understand it, and put it away.

Pru had the Lampers priced on her slate. "Lampers evens, us six-to-four against," she said. "Their man on L4 is Gil Fell. Sets once and sits. Steadiest Anchor in the league. Holds like a lamp bracket."
"Then why do they lose?" Lisbet said.
"They don't, much," said Pru.

We had the odd wall for Drop 1. I took L5, under Fell on L4. I took the lower ledge, as I always would now: what I carry pulls at a metre's reach, and I wanted it six metres from any Lap, not in one. Their other Anchor, a red-haired girl, held L2 true down, which costs nothing. Their Dropper, a light, quick lad called Ashby, beat Dunnet to the Cob and rode it down.

It came down through Fell's zone looking for all the world like a Cob in true down. It came out of the bottom of his zone moving toward our wall. I set L5 across against it for twenty counts. Half a head. Three pounds of carry I couldn't spare. It went into our well anyway.
Nought to three.

I scuffed the chalk flat round my boots and did the sum, and the sum wouldn't come out. Everything above Fell was true down. A Cob doesn't learn to go sideways in true down. So it had learned it in his zone. Fell wasn't holding true down at all. He was holding a hair off it, toward our wall, so near true that from the Lip it looked like nothing, and every metre a Cob fell through it walked it closer to our well, and he had been doing it all season and nobody had seen it.

In Drop 2 we had the even wall and I took L4, under Fell on L3, and I didn't fight his set. I let Dunnet bring the Cob down our own rope until he was below Fell's zone and in mine alone, and set L4 across at their wall for fifteen counts. Two heads. Seven pounds. Dunnet went down their wall into their well.
Three all.

At the Hoist the Weighman wrote two stone twelve and didn't look up. My bones said four stone ten. My knees said it too, in the sling. Heavy was a stone and four pounds away, and I had one Drop left to stay off it.
Pru called the coin and won it. I asked for the odd wall.

"Fell's set is off true toward our wall," I told them. "A few degrees. I don't know how many yet. Dunnet, take your chalk bag down with you and shake it when you come into his zone. I'll set L5 straight up from the bell, and when I see his chalk I'll match him exactly. Where his set and mine meet, under his ledge, nothing falls. You hang there with the Cob, and it costs nobody anything."
"Then the Letgo," said Lisbet.
"Then the Letgo."
"And when it rings he's over our well, with nothing to—"
"You'll bring him a line. Across their wall."
She looked at the far wall a long moment. "Move," she said, to herself.
Osk spoke from his chair without raising his voice, and all of us went quiet to hear it. "The Letgo's a place, I told you. Where's the place?"
"A long arm off the lip of Fell's ledge," I said. "Above the floor of it. Over their well."
"One: put it there." He waited, the way he does before the word that matters. "Two: keep it there. Three: let go."
"Fell's so steady they hang coats on him, don't they?" said Rafe, too loud, and Dunnet laughed for him, and I loved them both.
The bell.

The Weighman dropped the Cob through the Lid, and this time Dunnet had it before Ashby did, because he's twice Ashby's size and doesn't mind who he lands on. He came down our wall rope hand over hand with the Cob in the crook of his arm. I gripped L5 and turned it from true down to straight up. Six counts. My zone below the Lap was empty, so it cost nothing.
Fell's zone took Dunnet under L3. Dunnet opened the chalk bag at his belt and shook it.
A pinch of chalk fell past the L4 ledge and bent, very slightly, toward our wall.
Six degrees, or a hair under. I watched it slide while it crossed the Lap, and counted how far, and I was sure.
"Got you," I said.

I tipped my set six degrees toward their wall, straight up and a hair across, exactly opposite his. It's less than a count of turning. The chalk in the Lap stopped. It didn't fall and it didn't drift. It hung in the lamplight under Fell's ledge, a small grey cloud, and nothing moved it.

Dunnet came down into the cloud and stopped. He kept one hand on our rope, and the rope went slack, and he hung there, fifteen stone of him and the Cob, with nothing pulling either of them anywhere. Then he laughed, the big laugh, and it went all the way up the shaft.
"Counts," he called, "tell their lamp bracket he can stop now. We're comfortable."

In a null nothing falls, and holding a thing that doesn't fall costs nobody anything. Fell was paying nothing. I was paying nothing. But it only held because Dunnet held still. A man who had thrown two Drops for Teague was hanging in Shaft Nine with the match in his arm, and all he had to do to lose it was kick, and he didn't kick.
"Fell, across!" the Lampers' Caller shouted.

Fell turned. He's slow to start, Pru's book said, a man who sets once, but he started. The chalk round Dunnet pulled out into a grey thread toward our wall. Ashby was on their rope, not falling, so I could turn, and I followed the thread. Fell had a two-count start on me, and for two counts the Lap wasn't null and Dunnet swung on our rope, two heads, and Fell and I paid for it between us. A pound to me, or near it. Then the thread went back to a cloud.
Fell stopped turning. He doesn't like it.
"Two-to-one he sits!" Pru called from the Lip. "Two-to-one he sits for the rest of it!"
Two minutes ten. Dunnet was hanging off our rope, on our side of the shaft. If the Letgo rang with him there, the Cob would fall straight into our well, and we'd lose the match.

Lisbet was already on the far wall. She'd gone at the bell, round on the Lid ropes and down their side with a coil of line over her shoulder, and she was coming down toward Fell's ledge now, and I could hear her counting.
"Nine. Ten. The bolt. Eleven. Twelve, the crack. Thirteen."

She climbs with her eyes on the next hold. Always. I had watched her a hundred times in this shaft. Not on that wall. On that wall her face was turned up toward the lamp on their L2, and she was climbing by numbers.
She made her line fast to their fixed rope beside Fell's ledge with a rolling hitch. "Talk, Dunnet," she said. "Keep talking."
"I'm here, Lis. I'm the big thing by our wall. You can't miss me, I'm the size of a barge."
She threw the bight at his voice. It went a body's width wide of where he was, toward where the sound came off the wall, and Dunnet caught it only because his arms are long.

Then I knew. The lamp that burned clean in training, and her blaming it. The rope end that hit her shoulder against the Knockers. The far-wall calls she wanted shouted, not signed. She couldn't see the far wall. She could see Dunnet the way I can see the Lid from L5: a shape, and a voice. The league bars a Climber who can't see the far wall. She'd lose the league and the barge money and the rope-walk she wants, all of it, if anyone said it out loud.
It went into my throat and stuck there.

I wasn't going to say it. Not on the ledge, not at the Hoist, not to anyone. I know what it is to stand on a scale with a thing the book can't see. I wasn't going to be the one who read hers out. And holding it hurt, there under my jaw, every count of that Drop.

Dunnet let go of our rope and took her line in his free hand. Lisbet hauled. In a null a man weighs nothing, but he's still fifteen stone to start and fifteen to stop, and she brought him across hand over hand, slow, the way she'd bring a boat in. She stopped him knee-high to Fell, a long arm and a hand off the lip. She measured it with her own arm. Near things she sees fine.

Ashby came down onto Fell's ledge and lay flat and reached. His fingers came short of the Cob by a hand. He could have jumped for it. Then he'd have been drifting in the middle of the shaft with no rope when the warning rang, and he'd seen where the Cob was going to fall, and he'd have fallen with it. He stayed on the ledge.
"Four thirty!" Pru called.

My right hand was wet on the Pin. Three pounds in Drop 1, seven in Drop 2, one in the chase. Four stone eleven in my bones. A stone and three from Heavy. If Dunnet kicked, if Fell turned, if Lisbet's hitch slipped, I had nothing left to pay for it with.
The warning bell rang. One count.
Dunnet opened his arm. The Cob stayed where he left it, because nothing in a null moves unless something pushes it. He took the line in both hands.
Two counts.
"Cage standing, Da," I said. "Hold the brake."
I did the Release on the third count. Breathe in. Feel the Pin go quiet. Breath and hand together, little finger last.
Every Pin in the shaft let go, and for ten counts down was down.
The Cob fell. Ashby put his arm out over the lip as it went past, and it went past a hand beyond his fingers, straight down past their L6, and into their well.
Dunnet swung in on Lisbet's line and hit their wall under Fell's ledge with his shoulder, and held.
Six to three.

I sat down on L5 with my back to the wall. My knees went first and then the rest of me. I counted it, because counting is how I keep it out of my hands: eleven pounds for the match, and the null itself had cost nothing at all. Four stone of the other weight still in my bones, about two in the book. The eleven pounds would be gone by morning if I lay flat. The four stone would be five by next Monday, and nothing I could do on boards would touch it.
On the Lip the Weighman paid us five crowns each and didn't open the book. I put mine in Rafe's hand.
"Against the ninety-six," I said.
"You'll get a name for it, Dags," he said. "Girl who stood the Lampers still, isn't it?" His voice was steady and his eyes weren't.
Lisbet came up the ladder last, coiling her line. "Good reading, Quillon."
"Good line."
"Haig talks enough to throw at in the dark," she said, and laughed, and I watched her not look at the far wall, and said nothing. It was the hardest thing I did all day.
Teague was waiting at the rail. Soft grey coat, hat in his hand. He bowed to me a little, the way he does.

"A beautiful Drop, Dagny Quillon," he said. "Gil Fell has never been stood still in his life. I congratulate you." "Your brother's sum is ninety-six this morning. On Monday it will be one hundred, to the day."
"I know what it'll be," I said.

"Of course you do." He smiled. "Monday you play my Tallymen." He looked past me then, at Dunnet, who had gone still at the top of the ladder with the chalk still white on his sleeve. "They've asked after Dunnet Haig particularly."
